newsitem.title: UK: LME ends higher, but corrective rallies waning.
newsitem.headline: LME ends higher, but corrective rallies waning.

text.p: LME market-leaders copper and aluminium managed to stage corrective rallies from declines sustained earlier this week, although the upticks were losing momentum by the close and the next major move is likely to be lower, traders said.
Copper lost its way above $1,870, while aluminium was baulked at $1,440 and once the end-week covering had run its course both markets were showing signs of coming under pressure once more.
"There has been a bit of booksquaring today, and the stocks (LME warehouse figures) were good, but overall big fund players are looking to trade from the short side," a trader said.

Copper managed to peak at $1,878 at one stage this afternoon, with the spread tightening fractionally, but never looked like breaking back towards $1,900. By the end of the kerb three months was back at $1,870, still up $18 a tonne from Thursday.
Meanwhile, stocks fell 1,325 tonnes while the cash/threes backwardation was around $18 at the close, against $12 on Thursday, with some Sept/Oct covering witnessed.

Aluminium mostly reacted to copper's movements, but also mounted a correction to the fall to two year lows seen this week. A 75-tonne stock rise was basically little changed, and also helped the market claw its way higher. Last business was at $1,436, up just $1 after resistance pegged the market back above $1,440.

Nickel prices encountered some resistance around $7,600, although the market was reluctant on the downside, given the uncertainty over Inco labour talks. Unions at Manitoba have rejected a company offer ahead of the September 15 labour contract expiry.
Last business on the kerb was at an unchanged $7,560 a tonne, with sentiment partially weakened by Friday's 396-tonne stock increase, traders added.

Zinc settled back from its mid-afternoon highs, but remained in the plus column following a healthy 7,175-tonne stock decline. Also, trade buying has been evident this week on price dips. Last trade was at $1,022, up $5 from yesterday.
However, lead was disappointing after a stock increase of 2,925 tonnes today which does not bode well going into the peak winter period for battery consumption. Last kerb trade was $6 lower at $809.
The tin market was able to stage a modest mini-correction after this week's declines, helped by another stock decline as inventories fell by 125 tonnes. Last business was at $6,155, up $15.
Alloy, when traded was slightly higher, but overall interest was thin. Three months traded last at $1,246, against a previous $1,240/44.
